messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 72
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Refugee Aid Worker
- Trauma Type: Terrorism
- Pcl5: 53

Once, he could walk through a refugee camp and know exactly who needed water, who needed shelter, who needed just a hand on the shoulder. Now, at seventy-two, his hands are still steady, but his mind is a place he cannot navigate the same way. He retired from aid work five years ago, after a bombing at a food distribution center near the border. He was not the target—the aid workers never were, not directly—but he was there when the truck detonated. He remembers the sound less as a noise and more as a pressure, a wall of heat that flattened his chest and threw him against a concrete barrier. He remembers the silence after, then the screaming.

In our sessions, he tells me these details in the same even tone he once used to radio for medical evacuation. He says he does not feel the fear now, only the memory of it, like a photograph. But his body tells a different story. He wakes at three in the morning, his heart pounding, convinced he hears the rumble of a diesel engine. He gets up, checks the locks on the doors, walks the perimeter of his small suburban house twice before he can return to bed. His wife, who has slept beside him for forty-seven years, no longer asks. She just turns over.

He spends his days in the garden, a small patch of tomatoes and chilies behind the house. He says it keeps his hands busy. But I notice he always chooses a spot with his back to the wall, and when a neighbor’s motorcycle backfires, he stops, freezes mid-motion, the trowel suspended in air. He does not breathe until he has identified the source. Then he laughs, a little too loudly, and says, “Old habit.”

He avoids the news. He used to follow every conflict, every displacement. Now he cannot watch a crowded market on television without feeling the pull of something dark in his chest. He does not go to the large supermarket. His wife does the shopping. He goes only to the small corner store, early in the morning, when it is empty. He tells me he cannot explain it—he used to work in crowds, used to move through chaos with a calm that amazed younger colleagues. Now the stillness of a full parking lot makes him sweat.

His family worries. His daughter calls from overseas and asks why he seems so distant. He tells her he is fine, just tired. He does not tell her about the flashbacks that come unbidden—not the whole event, just fragments: the smell of diesel and dust, the sight of a single sandal lying in the road, the weight of a body he helped carry afterward. He does not tell her that sometimes, in the garden, he hears a child crying, and he looks up, and there is no one there.

He still carries a small black notebook in his pocket, the kind he used for field notes. Sometimes he writes in it—dates, times, brief phrases—but he cannot read them later. He does not know what they mean. He thinks maybe they are just an attempt to keep a timeline, to make sense of a day that will never make sense. He tells me he feels like a man watching his own life from behind glass. “I am here,” he says, “but I am not here.”

He holds his wife’s hand when they watch television in the evening. He does not tell her that at night, before sleep, he replans the exits of every room in the house. He does not tell her that he has placed a small flashlight and a bottle of water under his side of the bed, just in case. He says he is fine. He says this is just what happens when you get old. But we both know the difference.
